name: Britain
title: The Merchant Inside
pitch: No crown: a company, a school and coal towns inside Henry III's England.

core.n: London: the Company's wharves at Southwark
core.d: His base and the Company's gate. London is England's money, law and port; the south bank sits outside the City's guild rules but one bridge from its merchants. Later gates at Bristol (Severn, Forest of Dean) and Newcastle (coal).

start.n: Southwark, south end of London Bridge
start.d: Arrives in spring 1233 with nothing. Southwark is a busy suburb of inns, wharves and foreigners, so a strange man with an odd accent passes as just another merchant.

facts: ~3.5–4.5 million in 1230, rising to ~4.5–6 million by 1300 (historians disagree: Campbell ~4M c.1290, Broadberry et al ~4.75M c.1290)
Mild, wet, oceanic; the warm tail of the Medieval Warm Period. Cooler and wetter from ~1300 (Little Ice Age)
~550–700 mm in the south-east; 1,500–3,000 mm in the Welsh, Lake and Highland mountains; rain in every month
~7–8 months in the south (frost Nov–Mar); ~5–6 months in upland Scotland
Middle English (people), Anglo-Norman French (court and law), Latin (Church and records); Welsh, Cornish, Gaelic and Norse at the edges
Latin and French documents everywhere: charters, Exchequer pipe rolls, tally sticks, Roman numerals
Silver penny (sterling); 240 pence = £1. Credit from Jews and Italians
Henry III (b. 1207, king since 1216); personal rule from 1234

land.d: Heavy clay and river gravels around London, with marsh along the estuary. Good brick clay, poor drainage, malaria-like 'ague' (vivax) in the Thames and Essex marshes.
Wooded clay and sandstone between the chalk ridges of the North and South Downs. Iron ore in the clays, charcoal from the woods and steep streams for mill ponds; the Downs give sheep and lime.
Flat, fertile, crowded: Norfolk is the most populated county. The Fens are ~3,900 km² of peat and silt marsh, half wet in winter, rich in fish, fowl and reeds; marsh ague is common.
Open-field villages on heavy clay, the heart of English grain farming. Coal outcrops on its edges (Warwickshire, Staffordshire, Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire).
The moorland spine of the north: sheep, lead veins in the limestone, and fast streams. Coalfields lie on both flanks (Yorkshire east, Lancashire west, Durham north-east).
Limestone hills with England's best short-wool sheep, above the fertile Severn valley. The Severn is navigable from Bristol up past Gloucester to Shrewsbury.
Granite moors with tin in the valley gravels. Thin acid soils, small farms, mild winters by the sea.
Cattle and sheep country, few roads, hard to conquer. The south has a coastal plain and the great South Wales coalfield.
Fertile eastern lowlands (Lothian, Fife, the Merse) with coal by the Forth; the Highlands are thin-soiled, wet and pastoral, run by clans.
Mild and wet: grass grows almost all year, so cattle are wealth. Vast bogs in the middle, good tillage in the east and south-east (Leinster, Meath) where the Anglo-Normans settled.

peoples.culture: England's biggest town by far: merchants, guilds, a mayor (Andrew Bukerel, 1231–37) and aldermen, the royal court at Westminster nearby. English and French spoken; foreigners everywhere.
peoples.d: His market, his partners and his first customers. London backs whoever protects its liberties, as it later backs Montfort.

peoples.culture: Rich farm villages, Channel ports (the Cinque Ports), Canterbury's pilgrims. Freer than the Midlands: Kentish 'gavelkind' custom splits land between sons.
peoples.d: Close to London, holds the Weald iron and timber, and the ports to Flanders and France.

peoples.culture: The most crowded farmland in England, many free peasants, worsted cloth (named for Worstead), Yarmouth's herring fair, Flemish trade across the North Sea.
peoples.d: Grain, wool and weavers. Norwich has one of England's main Jewish communities.

peoples.culture: Sheep on the Wolds, fenland fishers and fowlers, rich abbeys (Crowland, Ramsey, Ely). Boston is a top wool port. Grosseteste becomes Bishop of Lincoln in 1235.
peoples.d: Fine long wool, the Fens to drain, and Grosseteste's seat.

peoples.culture: Classic open-field villages under manor lords, many villeins (unfree tenants owing labor). Market towns every ~10–15 km.
peoples.d: The biggest pool of serfs who might run to chartered towns, and coal on the edges.

peoples.culture: Rich valley farms; Oxford is a leading European university of Latin-speaking clerks, Franciscans (arrived 1224) and Dominicans (1221).
peoples.d: Where he finds Grosseteste and later Roger Bacon, and plants the Company's house of learning.

peoples.culture: Gloucestershire, Somerset, Wiltshire, Dorset and Devon: wool, cloth, cattle, dairying. Bristol trades with Ireland, Gascony and Wales.
peoples.d: Bristol is the port for the Forest of Dean and the Severn, the natural second gate.

peoples.culture: Cornish-speaking in the west, English in the east. Tinners have their own stannary courts and freedoms (charter of 1201). Richard of Cornwall becomes earl in 1227 and owns the tin revenue.
peoples.d: Tin and tinners who know water and digging; first customer for steam pumps.

peoples.culture: England's largest shire: Cistercian sheep abbeys (Fountains, Rievaulx), York's archbishop and merchants, Danish-flavored dialect.
peoples.d: Wool, Pennine water power and the Yorkshire coalfield. York's Jews were massacred in 1190, and the community had returned by the 1230s.

peoples.culture: Border country under the Prince-Bishop of Durham and border lords; cattle raiding with Scotland. Newcastle ships sea-coal and wool.
peoples.d: The coal coast. Newcastle's burgesses got a royal licence to dig coal around 1239.

peoples.culture: Royal property under the law: taxed at will by the Exchequer of the Jews. Moneylenders, pawnbrokers, physicians. Communities in London (Old Jewry), Lincoln, York, Norwich, Oxford, Winchester and others. Forced to wear a badge from 1218.
peoples.d: Literate, numerate and connected abroad; natural partners for finance and medicine, and a group the Company could shelter when pressure rises.

peoples.culture: Cologne Germans with their own Guildhall on the Thames, Flemings, Gascon wine men, Italian bankers and papal tax collectors.
peoples.d: His cover as a stranger, his rivals and his channels to Bruges, Lübeck and Italy. Also the people who will copy his products.

peoples.culture: Welsh-speaking cattle herders and farmers under Llywelyn the Great (d. 1240), Welsh law of Hywel Dda, bards, partible inheritance.
peoples.d: Independent until Edward I's conquest of 1277–83. A source of laborers and a war to stay out of.

peoples.n: Welsh Marches and 'Little England beyond Wales'
peoples.culture: Anglo-Norman marcher lords ruling mixed Welsh and English people; south Pembrokeshire was settled by Flemings in 1108 and still kept Flemish ways.
peoples.d: Covers the South Wales coalfield. Proof that Flemish settlers can be planted in Britain.

peoples.culture: Kingdom of Alexander II: burghs (Berwick is the richest), Scots English and French spoken, abbeys exporting wool, coal dug by monks near the Forth.
peoples.d: A peaceful neighbor in the 1230s (Treaty of York, 1237). War with England only from 1296.

peoples.culture: Gaelic-speaking clans and kindreds, cattle herding, galleys; the Western Isles are still under Norway until 1266.
peoples.d: Remote, poor, tough; fishermen and soldiers, little else for a 13th-century company.

peoples.culture: Norse-speaking earldom under the Norwegian crown; farmers, fishers and seafarers.
peoples.d: A stepping stone to Norway and the northern fisheries.

peoples.n: Kingdom of Mann and the Isles
peoples.culture: Norse-Gaelic island kingdom under Norway; passes to Scotland in 1266.
peoples.d: A small sea power in the Irish Sea.

peoples.culture: Ruled for Henry III from Dublin since 1171: castles, manors, English-speaking towns (Dublin, Waterford, Cork, Drogheda), grain and wool for export.
peoples.d: Food, hides, timber and room to grow. Overflow land for the Company later.

peoples.culture: Irish kings (O'Neill, O'Connor, O'Brien and others), Brehon law, cattle wealth and cattle raids, bards and learned families.
peoples.d: Mostly closed to outsiders; trade in cattle and hides through the ports.

resources.qty: modern: ~2,000 km² of field, ~57 seams; a 1925 survey put ~10.8 billion t within 1,200 m. Main seams ~1–2 m thick
resources.reach: 1230: seams outcrop along the Tyne banks and the Durham coast; dug in shallow pits and drifts, carried a few km to river staithes and shipped to London as 'sea-coal'
resources.d: The best coal for the job: right by navigable water and the sea. The obvious coal base and first wagonways.

resources.qty: modern: part of the Yorkshire–Notts–Derby field, Britain's largest; the Barnsley seam is ~2–3 m thick. Billions of t mined until 2015 (guess on total)
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops and shallow bell pits in the west of the field (Leeds, Wakefield, Barnsley); medieval digging recorded, mostly local use
resources.d: Huge but inland; reaches the sea down the Aire, Calder and Ouse to the Humber.

resources.qty: modern: southern half of the same giant field, several billion t (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops west of Nottingham; Nottingham coal is mentioned in the 1200s, the earliest surviving English coal lease is Cossall, 1316
resources.d: Coal near the Trent, which floats it to the Humber; also the Midland market.

resources.qty: modern: the 'Thick Coal' or Ten-Yard seam, up to ~9 m thick, the thickest in Britain; small field (~250 km²), long worked out
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops at the surface around Wednesbury and Dudley, next to clay ironstone and limestone
resources.d: Coal, iron ore and lime in one spot, but no navigable river: needs canals, as it did in history.

resources.qty: modern: ~2,600 km², Britain's largest continuous field; steam coal in the middle, anthracite in the west; billions of t mined (guess on total)
resources.reach: 1230: outcrops on the field's rim and along the coast near Swansea and Kidwelly; little dug, in marcher lords' land
resources.d: Coal and iron ore side by side by the Bristol Channel. Out of reach politically until the Company has marcher friends.

resources.qty: modern: rich hematite and goethite pockets in the Crease Limestone; >2 million t of ore raised in the bloomery era alone (Bick); mined until the 1940s
resources.reach: 1230: worked now by the 'free miners' in open pits ('scowles'); St Briavels castle makes crossbow bolts for the crown
resources.d: The best English iron ore, with coal, timber and limestone in the same forest and the Severn beside it. The variation's first Company town.

resources.qty: modern: small basin (~90 km²), thin seams; free mining still survives
resources.reach: 1230: shallow outcrops worked by the free miners under ancient custom
resources.d: Small but right next to the iron ore; enough to start coking trials.

resources.qty: modern: siderite nodules and bands in Cretaceous clays, ~25–35% iron (guess); ~680 bloomery sites and ~180 water-powered sites known
resources.reach: 1230: dug from minepits ~5 m wide and up to 12 m deep; smelted in small charcoal bloomeries
resources.d: The nearest iron to London, with endless coppice for charcoal and mill ponds for water power. Leaner ore than Dean.

resources.qty: modern: largely streamed out by the 1500s; small lodes remain
resources.reach: 1230: alluvial tin streamed from valley gravels; in 1213 Devon's tin revenue was farmed for more than Cornwall's
resources.d: Easier to reach from London by sea through Plymouth; declining as Cornwall rises.

resources.qty: modern: one of the world's great tin districts, ~2.5 million t of tin over all history (guess); lodes go down >500 m
resources.reach: 1230: tin streamed from valley gravels; England's smelted tin was ~300–400 t a year in the 13th century (Exeter study)
resources.d: Tin for pewter, bronze and solder. Deep lode mining needs pumps, which is why steam starts here.

resources.qty: modern: ~100,000 t of lead from the Mendips over all history (BGS); low silver
resources.reach: 1230: small rakes and pits in the limestone; the Bishop of Bath holds mining rights
resources.d: Lead for roofs, pipes, glazes and lead pans, close to Bristol.

resources.qty: modern: one of Europe's main lead fields; hundreds of thousands of t mined (guess). Little silver
resources.reach: 1230: worked in the King's Field under miners' customs and barmote courts; veins dug from the surface
resources.d: England's lead roofs and gutters; lead for chemistry and pewter.

resources.qty: modern: big lead-zinc field; the richest silver in medieval England
resources.reach: 1230: the 'silver mines of Carlisle' boomed in the 1130s–70s and still run at a smaller scale
resources.d: The one real English silver source; useful for the 1247 recoinage.

resources.qty: modern: a vast Triassic rock-salt bed, hundreds of m thick (found 1670); brine near saturation (~26% salt)
resources.reach: 1230: brine springs boiled in lead pans over wood fires in the 'wich' towns; Nantwich is the biggest
resources.d: Salt for meat, fish, butter and hides; later the base of soda and bleach chemistry.

resources.qty: modern: brine roughly ten times saltier than sea water
resources.reach: 1230: salt houses boiling brine since before Domesday; salt roads radiate across the Midlands
resources.d: The nearest strong brine to London by road; on the River Salwarpe near the Severn.

resources.qty: modern: England had ~10–15 million sheep by 1300 (guess); wool exports peaked ~35,000–45,000 sacks a year (~1 sack ≈ 165 kg)
resources.reach: 1230: sheep on every down and wold; the best fine wool from the Cotswolds, Herefordshire and Shropshire
resources.d: England's oil. Keeping the weaving at home turns raw wool into cloth worth several times more.

resources.qty: modern: the long-wool breeds of the Wolds and marsh
resources.reach: 1230: huge abbey flocks; Boston fair is one of the great wool markets
resources.d: Long staple for worsted and spinning wheels.

resources.qty: modern: England was ~15% wooded in 1086 (Rackham), less by 1300; the Weald is still England's most wooded region
resources.reach: 1230: managed coppice for charcoal and poles, oak for ships and houses; much is royal forest under forest law
resources.d: Charcoal for iron and glass. Firewood around London is already getting dear, which pushes coal.

resources.qty: modern: small remnants
resources.reach: 1230: large royal forests (Sherwood, Rockingham, Needwood); timber by royal grant only
resources.d: Big oak for mills, ships and roofs, but licenses come from the king.

resources.qty: modern: ~3,900 km² drained in the 1600s, now England's richest farmland
resources.reach: 1230: silt fens near the Wash already banked; peat fens flood each winter; abbeys own most of it
resources.d: The largest block of new farmland in England. Needs windmill or steam pumps and Dutch-style dykes.

resources.n: Thames and the river network (water power)
resources.qty: modern: Thames ~65 m³/s mean flow at London; England had ~5,600 water mills in Domesday (1086)
resources.reach: 1230: mills on every stream; fulling mills spreading; tide mills on estuaries
resources.d: Power is everywhere; the faster Pennine and Welsh streams are best for big mills later.

resources.qty: modern: England's grain belt
resources.reach: 1230: wheat, barley, oats, peas; yields ~4–5 times the seed (guess); barley for ale everywhere
resources.d: Feeds London. Clover, turnips and iron ploughs can lift yields a lot.

resources.qty: modern: the North Sea herring stock (collapsed in the 1970s, recovered)
resources.reach: 1230: the great autumn herring fair at Yarmouth; salted and smoked
resources.d: Cheap protein for Lent and winter; needs salt.

resources.n: London Clay and chalk (brick, tile, lime)
resources.qty: modern: London Clay is the base of London's brick industry; chalk Downs are hundreds of m thick
resources.reach: 1230: tile kilns exist; brick is rare (Coggeshall Abbey brick, ~1220s, is among England's first since Rome); chalk burned for lime
resources.d: Fire-safe brick and tile towns, lime mortar and later cement, all within a day of London.

resources.qty: modern: vast quarries
resources.reach: 1230: ragstone barged down the Medway to London; Purbeck marble for church columns; Caen stone imported from Normandy
resources.d: Stone for wharves, warehouses and furnaces.

resources.qty: modern: one of the world's main fuller's earth deposits (Nutfield, Redhill)
resources.reach: 1230: dug for cleaning and thickening cloth
resources.d: A cloth-finishing advantage right beside London.

resources.qty: modern: once the world's largest copper mine (1780s), ~3 Mt of ore with ~2–3% copper (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: Bronze Age and Roman workings, then forgotten; in Gwynedd's hands
resources.d: England's real copper for brass and wire; only reachable after Wales opens up.

resources.qty: modern: the Scottish Midland Valley coalfields, several billion t (guess)
resources.reach: 1230: monks of Newbattle and Dunfermline already dig outcrop coal by the Forth
resources.d: Coal by the sea in a friendly neighbor kingdom.

nearby.qty: modern: n/a; ~1300 Ghent ~50,000 and Bruges ~40,000+ people
nearby.reach: 1230: a day or two by sea; the biggest buyers of English wool and the best weavers, dyers and finishers in Europe
nearby.d: Market, rival and the source of skilled weavers. Bruges is the trade hub of the north.

nearby.qty: modern: the Meuse coal basin, mined until 1980
nearby.reach: 1230: coal is just starting to be dug near Liège (from the late 1100s)
nearby.d: The main coal rival on the Continent, but inland on the Meuse.

nearby.qty: modern: rich magnetite and hematite, often >50% iron; mined for 1,000+ years
nearby.reach: 1230: 'osmund' iron made in small furnaces, shipped by German traders from the Baltic
nearby.d: Very pure iron, later the best for steel. An import until Company iron beats it.

nearby.qty: modern: rich hematite (Somorrostro), ~50% iron; the base of Bilbao's steel industry
nearby.reach: 1230: worked in small forges; shipped by Castilian and Basque ships to England and Flanders
nearby.d: England's main imported iron in the Middle Ages.

nearby.reach: 1230: the Teutonic Knights arrive in Prussia in 1230; big grain exports come later in the century
nearby.d: Famine insurance. Richard of Cornwall's German grain saved London in 1258.

nearby.qty: modern: Norway's coastal cod and forests
nearby.reach: 1230: dried cod (stockfish), timber, tar and butter traded at Bergen; England–Norway treaty of 1217
nearby.d: Masts, planks, tar and cheap fish; a friendly kingdom.

nearby.n: Baltic tar, pitch and furs (Riga, Novgorod route)
nearby.reach: 1230: Riga founded 1201; wax, furs, tar and timber flow west through Gotland and Lübeck
nearby.d: Naval stores for a growing fleet.

nearby.qty: modern: n/a (the Øresund herring shoals faded in the 1500s)
nearby.reach: 1230: the biggest fish market in Europe each autumn, salted with Lüneburg salt
nearby.d: A competitor and a source of salted fish in famine years.

nearby.reach: 1230: cheap solar 'bay salt' shipped north; later the Hanse's main salt source
nearby.d: Cheaper than boiling brine with wood; a fallback for fish salting.

nearby.qty: modern: n/a; ~1300 Bordeaux shipped ~80,000–100,000 tuns a year (guess)
nearby.reach: 1230: Gascony is ruled by Henry III; wine ships sail to London and Bristol each autumn
nearby.d: England's main import and the reason for a big merchant fleet.

nearby.reach: 1230: Amiens merchants sell woad (blue dye) in London under royal privilege
nearby.d: Dye for the Company's cloth; madder and kermes come via Italians.

nearby.reach: 1230: alum comes via Italian merchants; Genoese take over Phocaea from 1275
nearby.d: Mordant needed to fix dyes. Expensive; a reason to learn to make it from local alum shales (Yorkshire coast, as in the 1600s).

nearby.qty: modern: ~27 million t of ore mined over 1,000 years
nearby.reach: 1230: Europe's great mine of the age, with skilled German miners
nearby.d: Copper for brass and wire, and a source of trained miners.

newcomers.num: thousands a year once Company towns exist (guess)
newcomers.d: English custom: a villein who lives a year and a day in a chartered borough is free. They already speak the language and know farm work; they need schooling and trades.

newcomers.when: from ~1240; waves after Flemish town revolts and the 1270–74 wool embargo
newcomers.d: England has wool but Flanders has the skill. Flemings already settled Pembrokeshire (1108) and trade in every east-coast port. Similar religion, food and farming.

newcomers.num: ~3,000–5,000 in England in the 1230s; ~2,000–3,000 expelled in 1290
newcomers.when: pressure throughout; the expulsion edict of 18 July 1290, departure by 1 November
newcomers.d: Under constant royal taxation, a 1218 badge rule, the 1275 Statute of the Jewry banning moneylending, and mass arrests and executions over coin-clipping in 1278–79. Most expelled went to France. The Company can employ them as financiers, doctors and clerks, mostly in its overseas offices, but English hostility is strong.

newcomers.num: a few dozen to a few hundred at most (guess); almost none reached England in history
newcomers.d: The Mongols wrecked Hungary and southern Poland and frightened the Baltic: in 1238 Gotland and Frisian fishermen skipped the Yarmouth herring fair. A few skilled Hungarian, Polish or German craftsmen or miners could be recruited via Cologne and Lübeck merchants.

newcomers.when: from ~1245, as Tyne, Dean and Cornish works grow
newcomers.d: Harz and later Bohemian miners know shafts, drainage and smelting. Historically they came to England in the 1500s. Cologne's Guildhall is the contact.

newcomers.when: throughout; more after the conquest of Wales (1283)
newcomers.d: Come for wages; different languages and laws, but long used to English markets and lords.

newcomers.when: throughout; more after French gains in 1242 and 1259
newcomers.d: Subjects of the same king, sailors and wine traders; French speakers who fit the merchant class.

newcomers.num: waves of thousands in bad years (guess)
newcomers.d: If Company grain stores hold when the Low Countries starve, skilled townspeople will cross. Easy cultural fit for Flemings and Frisians.

newcomers.when: throughout; Lucca and Florence firms in London from the 1220s
newcomers.d: Bankers, glassmakers and silk workers with the best accounting in Europe. Useful, but loyal to their own firms.

neighbors.d: Europe's industrial heart, living on English wool. Pulled between the French king (its overlord) and English trade. Its weavers will copy anything the Company makes within years; its town revolts send out refugees.

Europe's strongest kingdom, under a boy king and his mother Blanche of Castile until ~1234. Took Normandy from England in 1204 and wins again at Taillebourg (1242). Treaty of Paris (1259) brings peace; the Hundred Years' War starts in 1337.
Henry III's last big French land. Wine for wool and cloth; a ready Company office and a frequent cause of war with France.

At its peak under Haakon (r. 1217–63), holding Orkney, Shetland, the Hebrides and Man. Friendly trade treaty with England (1217). Loses the Hebrides and Man to Scotland in 1266. Increasingly dependent on German merchants for grain.

neighbors.n: German towns: Lübeck, Cologne and the coming Hanse
neighbors.d: Lübeck became an imperial free city in 1226; Cologne merchants hold a Guildhall in London. They control Baltic grain, timber, fur and Swedish iron, and will later win tax privileges in London (the Steelyard). Tough competitors, essential suppliers.
At peace with England: Alexander married Henry's sister Joan, and the Treaty of York (1237) fixed the border. Edward I's wars from 1296 make the north dangerous for 30 years.
The strongest Welsh prince, married to King John's daughter. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (Prince of Wales 1267) loses everything to Edward I in 1277–83.
Crowns united in 1230; Córdoba falls in 1236 and Seville in 1248. Source of Basque iron and merino wool (Castile guards its merinos). Edward I marries Eleanor of Castile in 1254.
Denmark lost its Baltic empire at Bornhöved (1227) but holds the Øresund and the Scania herring fair. Sweden is a loose kingdom with iron and copper (Falun is first recorded in 1288).
Frederick marries Henry III's sister Isabella in 1235; Richard of Cornwall is elected King of the Romans in 1257. Gives access to German miners and markets.

England has been a papal fief since 1213. Italian clerks hold English benefices, sparking riots in 1231–32. The Church can excommunicate; an unorthodox merchant must look pious and stay on Grosseteste's right side.
Conquers the Rus' 1237–40 and crushes Poland and Hungary in 1241, then withdraws in 1242. No threat to England, but it scares Baltic traders and sends a few refugees west.
